fable-5.1.text:
I think the significance is a bit different from how people usually frame it. The common story is that attention beat convolution, and that's why ViT was a big deal. I actually don't think that's the main reason.

To me the breakthrough is that, for the first time, vision could use basically the same architecture as language. Before that, every modality had its own specialized design. Vision had ConvNets with all these built-in inductive biases: locality, translation equivariance, hierarchical feature maps. Language had RNNs and then transformers. Those worlds didn't really talk to each other at the architecture level. Once ViT showed that a plain transformer operating on image patches could match or exceed ConvNets, given enough data, it became possible to think about one model family for everything. That's what made things like CLIP and later the multimodal LLMs so natural. You tokenize whatever you have, you feed it into the same kind of network, and you train it the same way.

The second thing is scaling. ViT made it very clear that if you remove a lot of the hand-designed priors and just give the model more data and more compute, it keeps improving. That changed the mindset of the field. People stopped asking "what is the right inductive bias for images" and started asking "what is the right recipe for training at scale."

Now, I'll say this with the ConvNeXt work in mind. When we went back and modernized a ResNet with the same training recipe and design decisions that transformers brought in, the gap mostly disappeared. So a lot of what people attributed to attention was really about the training procedure, the larger kernels, the normalization choices, the macro design. In that sense the transformer was almost more important as a catalyst than as a specific mechanism. It forced the community to re-examine assumptions that had been frozen for years, and that re-examination improved ConvNets too.

So if you ask me why it's an important breakthrough, I'd say it's less that transformers are intrinsically better for images, and more that they unified the field and shifted everyone toward scale and simplicity. That shift is the thing that has persisted.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly identifies using the same architecture and tokenization approach for vision and language, enabling a unified model family across text and images.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important part isn't that transformers beat convolutional networks on ImageNet by some margin. It's what they did to the field as a whole.

For almost a decade, from AlexNet through ResNet and DenseNet, computer vision had its own architecture family. Convolutions were seen as the natural fit for images, with their locality and translation equivariance. NLP had moved to transformers, and the two communities were evolving fairly separately. When Vision Transformer came out, it showed that you could take an architecture designed for language, cut an image into patches, treat them like tokens, and with enough data and compute get excellent results. That was a big conceptual shift. It suggested that a lot of the hand-designed inductive bias we thought was essential for vision could be learned from data at scale.

The biggest consequence is unification. Once vision and language share the same backbone, it becomes much easier to build multimodal systems. You can feed image tokens and text tokens into the same model, share infrastructure and training tricks, and transfer scaling insights from one domain to the other. Much of what we see today in vision-language models, and in models that handle images, video and text together, depends on that common architectural language.

The second reason is scaling. Transformers turned out to scale very gracefully with data and parameters, and they pair naturally with self-supervised objectives like masked image modeling. That opened a path to the kind of large-scale pretraining that had transformed NLP.

That said, I'd be careful about the narrative that attention is simply better than convolution. Part of the motivation for our ConvNeXt work was to ask how much of the gain came from self-attention itself versus everything else that came with it: the training recipes, data augmentation, longer training, layer normalization, larger kernels, the macro design of the network. When we modernized a standard ResNet step by step with those design choices, a pure ConvNet could match or exceed Swin Transformers at similar scales. So I see the transformer moment partly as a forcing function. It made the community revisit assumptions, adopt much better training practices, and think more carefully about what actually matters in architecture design.

So to me the breakthrough is a mix of things: proving that a general-purpose architecture works for vision, enabling unification with language, and shaking up a field that had become fairly settled in its ways. All three have been very healthy for computer vision.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly identifies unification as a major consequence, explaining that vision and language can share a backbone and that image and text tokens can be processed in the same model.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. So, it's interesting — a lot of people assume the breakthrough was purely about accuracy, like transformers suddenly made models much better at ImageNet. But actually, if you look carefully, with careful design a ConvNet can be quite competitive on many of those benchmarks — that was part of what we showed with ConvNeXt. To me, the real significance of transformers in vision is something different: it's unification.

Before ViT, vision and language were essentially separate worlds architecturally. You had ConvNets on one side, recurrent models and then transformers on the other, and the communities had their own tricks, their own training recipes. Once vision adopted transformers, suddenly everything speaks the same language — an image becomes a sequence of tokens, just like text. That's what makes modern multimodal models possible. You can feed images, text, audio, even video into essentially the same architecture, and that's a huge deal for building general-purpose models.

The second thing is flexibility. Transformers have relatively weak inductive biases, which sounds like a disadvantage, but it means the model learns more from data, and it handles things like masked modeling very naturally — MAE is a great example. You can drop patches, mix modalities, do in-context tasks, and the architecture doesn't fight you.

So my view is: the breakthrough wasn't "attention beats convolution" on some benchmark. It was that vision joined a shared, scalable framework, and that reshaped the whole trajectory of the field.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly identifies unification: images become sequences of tokens like text, allowing vision and language to use a shared architectural framework.

opus-5.text:
It's a good question, and my answer is probably a little different from the standard one.

I don't think the important thing was self-attention as an operator. When ViT came out, the headline reading was "attention beats convolution," and a lot of people took that literally. But if you look carefully at those comparisons, a huge amount was changing at once — the training recipe, the augmentation, the regularization, the optimizer, the amount of pre-training data, the patchify stem. We did some of this work with ConvNeXt, basically asking: if you take a ResNet and modernize it along all those axes, how much of the gap is left? And the answer was, not much. You can get a pure convolutional network to match Swin and ViT across image classification, detection, segmentation. So the empirical claim that attention is intrinsically the better inductive bias for pixels — I think that was substantially confounded.

What was genuinely a breakthrough is two things. The first is conceptual: ViT showed that an architecture with almost no vision-specific prior — no locality, no hierarchy, barely any translation equivariance — could be competitive, provided you gave it enough data. The field had spent twenty years hand-designing priors into vision models, and this was strong evidence that priors are a substitute for data, not a requirement. When data is scarce they help; when data is abundant they're a constraint you're paying for. That reframing changed what questions people thought were worth asking.

The second is more mundane and probably more consequential: unification. Once vision, language, audio, and video all run through the same architecture, everything becomes shared. The kernels, the distributed training infrastructure, the scaling laws people worked out for language, the engineering effort — it all transfers. And multimodal models stop being an integration problem and become almost trivial, because you're just feeding different token streams into the same stack. I don't think you get the current generation of vision-language models without that. That was never really an argument about accuracy on ImageNet; it was an argument about what the field could build on top.

So the way I'd put it: the breakthrough was real, but it was a breakthrough about scale, priors, and shared substrate — not about one operator being better than another. And I think it's worth being precise about that, because the lesson you draw determines whether you spend the next five years tweaking attention variants or thinking about data.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes vision and language using the same architecture and shared token-processing stack, enabling multimodal models; this communicates unification of text and image representations as a benefit.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's important, though maybe not for the reason people usually give. The common story is that transformers beat ConvNets on ImageNet, so they're better. When we worked on ConvNeXt, we found that if you modernize a ConvNet with the same training recipe, the same data augmentation, and some of the same macro design choices, it gets very close to a vision transformer on standard benchmarks. So on pure accuracy, I don't think the gap was as large as it first looked.

What I do think mattered is that vision stopped being its own separate world. Before ViT, the vision community had its own architectures, with convolutions, pooling, and inductive biases that we hand-designed for images. Language had moved to transformers, and the two fields were building very different tools. Once you can take an almost unmodified transformer, cut the image into patches, and have it work well, you get a shared architecture across modalities. That makes it much easier to do multimodal work, to share research progress and infrastructure, and to scale things up the same way people were scaling language models.

Scaling is the other piece. Transformers were very well suited to large-scale pretraining, and the tooling and hardware optimization grew up around them. Some of the advantage is that the whole ecosystem is built around this architecture, not that it's intrinsically better for images.

So I'd say it was a breakthrough in terms of unification and in showing that you don't need strong vision-specific priors if you have enough data and compute. But I wouldn't say convolution was wrong. That's why we wanted to ask, with ConvNeXt, how much of the improvement came from the architecture and how much from everything else around it.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes unifying language and vision through a shared transformer architecture across modalities, enabling multimodal work and shared research infrastructure.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the main contribution wasn't that attention is inherently better at seeing images. Convolutions came with strong built-in assumptions, mainly locality and translation equivariance. Those help a lot when data is limited, but they also tie the architecture to a particular set of design choices. The transformer treated an image as a sequence of patches, using the same basic machinery that already worked well for language. That made the architecture far more general and let the field converge on one backbone.

What mattered most to me was scaling. Once you have a flexible architecture that keeps improving with more data and compute, the bottleneck moves from architecture design to data and training recipes. That shift made large pretrained vision models practical, and it's a big reason vision and language now share so much infrastructure.

I'd add a caveat, though. Much of the performance gap people attributed to attention came from training recipes and macro design choices. When you bring those same choices to a convolutional network, it can be quite competitive. So I don't think transformers won because convolutions are fundamentally inferior. They won partly because they arrived with a clean, scalable recipe that the community rallied around.

r001.rationale: The response states that transformers represent images as sequences of patches using the same machinery as language, enabling shared vision-and-language infrastructure; this clearly conveys unification of text and image representations.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest breakthrough is that it showed we could use essentially the same architecture across different modalities. Traditionally, computer vision had convolutional networks, and language modeling had its own architectures. A lot of our work in vision went into designing structures specifically for images.

With transformers, you can represent an image as a sequence of patches and use a very similar architecture to the one used for language. That challenges the idea that you need a highly specialized architecture for each kind of data. You can let the model learn more of those relationships, given enough data and the right training.

And that creates a really useful connection between fields. Improvements in architectures and training methods can transfer more easily between language and vision. It also makes combining the two more natural. So, to me, the significance goes beyond better image classification accuracy—it’s a step toward a more unified way of building models.

r001.rationale: The response clearly describes using a shared transformer architecture and representing images as patch sequences analogous to language, framing this as a unified approach across text and vision.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important part is that it showed we could use essentially the same architecture for vision and language. Traditionally, computer vision relied heavily on convolutional networks, which build in assumptions about images—for example, that nearby pixels are especially related and that the same pattern can appear at different locations.

Transformers have fewer of those image-specific assumptions, so more of that structure has to be learned from data. That makes the question of scale really interesting: how much can you gain by increasing the data and computation, instead of carefully designing the architecture for each task?

And having a common architecture makes it easier to bring images and language together. To me, that opens up a much broader direction than just improving accuracy on an image classification benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response states that transformers enable a common architecture for vision and language and make it easier to bring images and language together, clearly conveying unified text-and-image representations.

sol-6.text: I think it was a breakthrough because it changed how we approach vision. Instead of building in so many assumptions about how an image should be processed, transformers let a model learn relationships between different parts of the image through attention. That also brought vision closer to the methods used in language, making it easier to study how these models scale and how they can work across both kinds of data.

r001.rationale: The response says vision became closer to language methods and could work across both data types, but it does not clearly identify unifying text and image representations as the benefit.

terra-5.6.text: I think it was a really important moment because, for a long time, computer vision relied almost entirely on convolutional networks. Convolutions build in very strong assumptions about locality and translation invariance, which are useful, but they also make vision models quite different from language models. Transformers showed that, given enough data and scale, you can use a much more general architecture for images and get very competitive—or better—results. That opens the door to a more unified way of thinking about vision, language, and multimodal learning, rather than designing a separate architecture for every domain.

sol-5.6.text: I think it was important because it showed that computer vision didn’t have to rely on the strong inductive biases built into convolutional networks. Transformers offered a much more general architecture that could learn relationships across an entire image and, just as importantly, could scale very effectively with data and computation. That helped unify vision with language under a similar modeling framework and opened the door to large multimodal models, where images and text can be processed and learned together.

luna-5.6.text: I think it was important because it changed the basic way we think about visual representation. Convolutional networks build in a strong local, hierarchical bias, whereas transformers can directly model relationships between distant image regions. That makes the architecture much more flexible and, importantly, gives us a common framework that scales with data and compute and can connect naturally to language and other modalities. In practice, this shift has made it possible to train increasingly general-purpose vision models rather than designing a new architecture for every task.

luna-6.text: I think the important part was that transformers showed we could rethink some assumptions about vision. Convolutions give you a really useful built-in bias toward local patterns, and for a long time that was central to how we designed vision models. But with enough data and compute, transformers could learn those relationships from the data while also connecting information across an image more directly. That opened up a simpler, more scalable way to build models, and eventually a shared architecture across language and vision. The breakthrough wasn’t that transformers are always better; it was that they expanded what we thought was possible.
